name: Sukhia Pokhari
tagline: The market junction where roads split for Mirik and Sandakphu
meta_description: Sukhia Pokhari near Darjeeling: the 'dry pond' market town, jeep junction for Mirik and Maneybhanjan, Simana viewpoint, Pashupati market, fares and tips.
summary: Sukhia Pokhari is a hill market town and block headquarters at about 2,100 m, roughly 20 km from Darjeeling via Ghoom. It is the junction for Mirik, Maneybhanjan and the Sandakphu trek, Jorepokhri and Lepchajagat. Stop for momos and market life, the Simana viewpoint into Nepal and cheap shared jeeps in every direction.

local_story.title: A dry pond at the crossroads of the ridge
paras: The usual reading of the name is plain Nepali: sukhia, dry, and pokhari, pond. Ask which pond, and why it was dry, and you will get different answers; we have not found a written source that settles it. What is clear is the town's job. Sukhia Pokhari sits on the ridge west of Ghoom where the roads split: one runs on to Maneybhanjan and the Singalila Ridge, one down via Simana to Mirik, one to Jorepokhri and the tea gardens. People have changed jeeps, traded and eaten at this junction for as long as the roads have run here.

That makes it a working town rather than a resort. It is the headquarters of a community development block of Darjeeling district, with government offices, schools and a market where farmers from the surrounding villages sell potatoes, vegetables and milk and buy rice, cloth and tools. Trekkers bound for Sandakphu pass through on the way to Maneybhanjan, a short drive on. Indian shoppers head the other way, to the border at Simana and the market at Pashupatinagar in Nepal.

The border is part of its story. The ridge here runs close to Nepal, and the hills of Ilam, known across Nepal for their tea, lie just across. People on both sides share a language, festivals and often family ties, and goods move both ways through Pashupatinagar every day. Standing at Simana, whose name is simply the Nepali word for border, and looking west over a different country, you understand how thin the line on the map feels to the people who live along it.

did_you_know: Sukhia Pokhari's name is usually read as 'dry pond', from Nepali sukhia (dry) and pokhari (pond); locals give different accounts of which pond and why it dried.
Maneybhanjan, the road head for the Singalila Ridge trek to Sandakphu (3,636 m, the highest point in West Bengal), is a short drive beyond Sukhia Pokhari.
Simana, the viewpoint on the Sukhia Pokhari to Mirik road, takes its name from the Nepali word for border and looks into Nepal's Ilam district, known for its tea.
intro: Most people see Sukhia Pokhari through a jeep window on the way to Mirik or Maneybhanjan. That is a pity, because it is one of the best places in the hills to watch ordinary life rather than tourism. The main road is lined with shops, tea stalls and momo kitchens; jeeps load and unload with sacks, schoolchildren and trekkers; and in the mornings farmers come in from the villages with vegetables and leave with rice and cloth. At about 2,100 m it is as cool as Darjeeling and far less crowded.

Use it as a junction and a half-day stop. From here the Simana viewpoint looks into Nepal, Pashupati market is a short ride beyond, the twin ponds of Jorepokhri are 4 km away and Lepchajagat's forest is a few kilometres back toward Ghoom. Trekkers bound for Sandakphu pass through on the way to Maneybhanjan. Shared jeeps are cheap: ₹70–100 to Darjeeling, with similarly small fares onward to Mirik and Maneybhanjan.

highlights.title: The market on the main road
highlights.text: Shops, stalls and small kitchens line the road through town, selling everything from potatoes and greens to blankets, shoes and school bags. Come in the morning, when farmers from the villages are in town, and eat momos at a stall while jeeps load around you.

highlights.title: Simana viewpoint
highlights.text: On the road toward Mirik, Simana, the Nepali word for border, looks west into the Ilam hills of Nepal, with tea gardens and villages on the slopes. Clear mornings from October to April are best, and tea stalls make it an easy 20–30 minute stop.

highlights.title: Pashupati market across the border
highlights.text: Indian citizens with valid photo ID usually cross at Pashupatinagar to shop in Pashupati market for clothes, shoes, blankets and packaged goods. No visa is needed; foreigners generally cannot cross here. Rules and checks change, so check current status before you travel.

highlights.title: Jorepokhri's twin ponds
highlights.text: Four kilometres away, Jorepokhri was declared India's first salamander sanctuary in 1985. Recent reporting says the newts no longer breed in its altered ponds, but the forest setting and the story still make a good short visit or an easy walk.

highlights.title: The road to Maneybhanjan and Sandakphu
highlights.text: Maneybhanjan, the road head for the Singalila Ridge trek to Sandakphu and Phalut, is a short jeep ride on. Many trekkers come through Sukhia, buy last snacks and gloves and carry on. Guides, park entry and Land Rovers are arranged in Maneybhanjan.

highlights.title: Lepchajagat's forest
highlights.text: A few kilometres back toward Ghoom, Lepchajagat's conifer and rhododendron forest gives quiet walks, birds and a dawn view of Kanchenjunga. Combine it with Sukhia on a half-day, or stay there instead for a night in the forest.

how_to_reach.text: Jeeps for Sukhia Pokhari, Mirik and Maneybhanjan leave from Darjeeling's motor stand through the day, most often in the morning. Sukhia is about 20 km, roughly an hour via Ghoom and Lepchajagat, at ₹70–100 a seat.

From Siliguri, take a shared jeep to Mirik, then a Darjeeling-bound jeep that runs via Simana and Sukhia Pokhari. It is cheaper than a reserved car and a scenic route, though slower with the change. Afternoon jeeps are fewer, so check timings locally.

A car from Darjeeling costs ₹1,500–2,500 for a half-day with Lepchajagat, Jorepokhri and Simana. From NJP or Bagdogra, a reserved car to Sukhia Pokhari costs about ₹3,500–4,500 via Mirik or via Ghoom, around 3–3.5 hours.

where_to_stay: Sukhia Pokhari is a market town, not a resort, and most travellers do not sleep here. If you need a bed in town, ask at the jeep stand about simple rooms and look before you pay, because standards vary. For a better night nearby, go 4 km to Jorepokhri Tourist Lodge, run by the GTA beside the twin ponds, or back toward Ghoom to Lepchajagat, where the WBFDC resort and village homestays charge about ₹1,500–2,500 per person with meals. Trekkers usually sleep at Maneybhanjan, a short ride on, before starting for Sandakphu, or come straight from Darjeeling.
tips: Arrive in the morning, when the market is busiest and onward jeeps to Mirik and Maneybhanjan run most often.
Carry valid photo ID such as a passport or voter ID if you plan to visit Pashupati market across the border.
Ask the fare before you take a jeep seat; local fares are fixed and other passengers will confirm them.
Buy last-minute trek basics such as gloves, socks and snacks here if you are heading to Maneybhanjan and Sandakphu.
Leave for Darjeeling by mid-afternoon, since shared jeeps thin out toward evening.

experiences.title: Market morning and momos in Sukhia Pokhari
experiences.summary: A slow morning in Sukhia Pokhari's market: farmers in from the villages, jeeps loading in three directions, and momos, aloo dum and milky tea in roadside kitchens. Hill life without the tourist gloss, for under ₹300.
body: Sukhia Pokhari is a working junction, and its market shows how the western Darjeeling hills actually live. Along the main road you find vegetable sellers with potatoes, cabbages, chillies, squash and greens from the surrounding villages; shops stacked with rice sacks, blankets, school bags and plastic buckets; hardware, medicines and mobile recharge counters; and small kitchens with a pot of momos steaming at the front. In the mornings the road fills with people who have come in from the villages for the day.

Arrive by 8 or 9 am, by shared jeep from Darjeeling or Mirik, and walk the length of the market slowly. Eat as you go: a plate of momos for ₹80–150, a bowl of thukpa or aloo dum, a cup of milky tea for ₹20–40, and sel roti, the ring-shaped rice bread, if someone is frying it. Look for chhurpi, the hard dried cheese chewed slowly like a sweet, and for local pickles in jars. Prices here are lower than in Darjeeling's tourist lanes.

Be polite with photographs, especially of people at work, and ask first. Buy something small from the farmers if you can; even a bag of oranges in winter or a packet of dried chillies puts money where it counts. Then use the junction: jeeps run on to Maneybhanjan, down to Mirik via Simana and back to Darjeeling. If you have time, take a local car to Jorepokhri and Simana before lunch, and come back to the market for a second plate of momos.

faqs.q: Is there a weekly market day in Sukhia Pokhari?
faqs.a: Shops and stalls open daily, and the town is busiest on weekday mornings. Many hill towns also hold a weekly haat when more farmers come in, but days can change, so ask your driver or at a tea stall. Even on an ordinary morning there is plenty to see and eat.

faqs.q: Is the street food safe to eat?
faqs.a: Generally yes, if you choose busy stalls where food is cooked fresh in front of you, such as steamed momos and hot thukpa. Avoid raw salads and unboiled water, and carry bottled or filtered water. If your stomach is sensitive, start with steamed rather than fried food on the first day.

faqs.q: What should we eat in Sukhia Pokhari?
faqs.a: Momos, steamed or fried, with chilli sauce; thukpa or noodle soup; aloo dum; sel roti if anyone is frying it; and milky tea. In winter look for local oranges. Try hard chhurpi, the dried cheese chewed slowly like a sweet, but go gently on your teeth.

experiences.title: Across the border to Pashupati market
experiences.summary: A half-day from Sukhia Pokhari past the Simana viewpoint to the border at Pashupatinagar, where Indian visitors with ID walk across to shop in Pashupati market. Views of Nepal's Ilam hills on the way and cheap everyday goods at the end.
body: India and Nepal share an open border, and the ridge west of Sukhia Pokhari is one of the places where you can feel it. Drive out along the Mirik road to Simana, whose name is Nepali for border, and the land drops away into the Ilam hills of eastern Nepal, a district known for its tea. A little further on is the crossing to Pashupatinagar, a Nepali border town whose market draws shoppers from the Darjeeling hills for clothes, shoes, blankets, packaged food and household goods.

Indian citizens can usually walk across without a visa, carrying valid photo ID such as a passport or voter ID card; children may need a school ID or birth certificate. Foreign nationals generally cannot use this crossing and should not try. Security staff may check bags and ID on both sides. Rules, timings and checks change, sometimes at short notice around elections or holidays, so carry ID for everyone in your group and check current status before you travel.

Go by local car from Sukhia for ₹600–1,200 return with waiting, or fold it into a Darjeeling to Mirik day tour. Stop at Simana for tea and the view first, while the light is clear, then cross for an hour or two of shopping. Indian rupees are widely taken, but carry ₹100 and ₹200 notes, since larger Indian notes have at times been refused in Nepal. Respect customs limits on what you bring back, and do not photograph border posts.

faqs.q: Can foreigners visit Pashupati market?
faqs.a: Generally no. The Pashupatinagar crossing is used by Indian and Nepali citizens, and foreign nationals are not normally allowed to cross here; the usual crossing for other nationalities near Siliguri is Panitanki to Kakarbhitta. Foreigners can still enjoy the Simana viewpoint on the Indian side. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What currency is used at Pashupati market?
faqs.a: Nepali rupees are the local currency, but Indian rupees are widely accepted at border markets, at the fixed rate of about 1.6 Nepali rupees to one Indian rupee. Carry ₹100 and ₹200 notes, since larger Indian notes have at times been refused in Nepal. Do not rely on cards.

faqs.q: What can we buy at Pashupati market?
faqs.a: Mostly everyday goods: clothes, jackets, shoes, blankets, bags, packaged snacks and household items, often a little cheaper than in Darjeeling. Some visitors buy Nepali tea from Ilam. Check quality carefully, keep receipts if given, and stay within customs limits on what you carry back into India.

experiences.title: Walk the 4 km to Jorepokhri's twin ponds
experiences.summary: A 4 km road walk from Sukhia Pokhari's market to the twin ponds of Jorepokhri, through forest and past tea, with the honest story of India's first salamander sanctuary at the end. About an hour each way at an easy pace.
body: Most people drive to Jorepokhri. Walking is better. The road from Sukhia Pokhari runs about 4 km through mixed forest and along the edge of the tea, with little traffic and long views over the ridges when the cloud allows. It climbs gently for much of the way, so the outward walk takes about an hour and the return a little less. You pass village houses, small shrines and the odd tea shop, and you arrive at the ponds warm, which helps at about 2,250 m.

At the ponds, walk the short path around both pools and read the boards about the Himalayan salamander. Jorepokhri was declared India's first salamander sanctuary in 1985. Be clear about what you will not see: according to 2026 reporting by Mongabay, concrete paving and tourist works have changed the ponds so much that the newts no longer breed here. The setting is still quiet and green, and the lesson about how good intentions can damage a habitat stays with you.

Start mid-morning, after the market, and carry water and a rain jacket, because mist can roll in by noon. Walk on the outer edge of the road and keep children close, as jeeps come quickly round the bends. If your legs give out, ask at the ponds for a local car back to Sukhia; it will cost a few hundred rupees. Back in town, momos and tea are waiting, and the jeeps for Darjeeling and Mirik leave from the same stand.

faqs.q: How long does the walk from Sukhia Pokhari to Jorepokhri take?
faqs.a: About an hour each way at an easy pace for the roughly 4 km road, a little longer uphill if you stop for views and tea. With half an hour at the ponds, the whole outing takes about 2.5 to 3 hours. Start by mid-morning to finish before the afternoon mist.

faqs.q: Is the road walk to Jorepokhri safe?
faqs.a: Yes, with normal road sense. It follows a quiet road with light traffic, but jeeps take bends fast, so walk single file on the outer edge where you can see and be seen. Wear something bright in mist, carry a torch in winter when dark comes early, and avoid walking after dusk.

faqs.q: Can we get a vehicle back if we are tired?
faqs.a: Usually, yes. Local cars come to Jorepokhri with visitors, and drivers at the lodge or parking area will often take you back to Sukhia Pokhari for a few hundred rupees. Do not count on it late in the day; take a driver's number from Sukhia's stand as a backup.

experiences.title: Last market stop before the Singalila Ridge
experiences.summary: Use Sukhia Pokhari as the last market stop before Maneybhanjan, the road head for Sandakphu and Phalut on the Singalila Ridge. Buy small supplies, take a cheap shared jeep on, and sort out guide and park entry in Maneybhanjan.
body: The Singalila Ridge trek to Sandakphu, at 3,636 m the highest point in West Bengal, starts at Maneybhanjan, a small border town a short drive beyond Sukhia Pokhari. From Sandakphu on a clear day you see Kanchenjunga at close range and Everest, Lhotse and Makalu far to the west. Most trekkers reach Maneybhanjan from Darjeeling, and almost all of them pass through Sukhia on the way. For budget trekkers it is a useful place to change jeeps, buy supplies and eat a proper meal.

Use the market to fill gaps in your kit: woollen socks, gloves, a hat, a cheap rain poncho, energy snacks, a torch with spare batteries and a refillable bottle. Prices are lower than in Darjeeling's tourist lanes. Then take a shared jeep on to Maneybhanjan for roughly ₹40–70 a seat. In Maneybhanjan you register, pay the Singalila National Park entry and hire a licensed guide, which is compulsory inside the park; Land Rovers for the road to Sandakphu are arranged there too.

Rules, fees and guide rates on the Singalila Ridge change, and roads on the ridge can close after heavy rain or snow, so check current status before you travel. If you arrive late, sleep in Maneybhanjan rather than starting to walk in the afternoon. Coming back down, Sukhia is also where many trekkers stop for their first hot momos after days of dal and rice on the trail, before the last jeep ride to Darjeeling.

faqs.q: How far is Maneybhanjan from Sukhia Pokhari?
faqs.a: It is a short drive along the ridge road, roughly 20–30 minutes by shared jeep. Jeeps run most often in the morning. Many trekkers come straight from Darjeeling to Maneybhanjan in one jeep, a trip of about 26 km and 1.5 hours that passes through Sukhia without stopping.

faqs.q: Do we need a guide for Sandakphu?
faqs.a: Yes. A licensed guide is compulsory inside Singalila National Park and is hired at Maneybhanjan along with your park entry. Guide fees are set per day and change from season to season. Check current status before you travel, and agree the number of days and what is included in writing.

faqs.q: Can we buy trekking gear in Sukhia Pokhari?
faqs.a: Basic items, yes: socks, gloves, woollen hats, ponchos, torches, batteries and snacks. Do not expect technical gear, good boots or sleeping bags. Bring serious equipment from home or Siliguri, or hire it in Darjeeling, and use Sukhia only for last-minute small things.

faqs.q: How far is Sukhia Pokhari from Darjeeling?
faqs.a: About 20 km, roughly an hour by road via Ghoom and Lepchajagat. Shared jeeps from Darjeeling's motor stand bound for Sukhia, Mirik or Maneybhanjan cost about ₹70–100 a seat. A reserved car for a half-day with Jorepokhri and the Simana viewpoint costs ₹1,500–2,500.

faqs.q: What does Sukhia Pokhari mean?
faqs.a: It is usually read as 'dry pond', from Nepali sukhia, dry, and pokhari, pond. Local people give different explanations of which pond is meant and why it was dry, and we have not found a written source that settles it. You will also see the name written as Sukhiapokhri or Sukhia Pokhri.

faqs.q: Is Sukhia Pokhari worth visiting?
faqs.a: As a stop, yes. It is a real hill market town and the junction for Mirik, Maneybhanjan, Jorepokhri and Lepchajagat. Spend an hour or two in the market, then visit Simana and Jorepokhri. As a place to spend several days it has little to offer; sleep at Lepchajagat or Jorepokhri instead.

faqs.q: How do we get from Sukhia Pokhari to Mirik?
faqs.a: Shared jeeps run from Sukhia toward Mirik through Simana, taking roughly 1 to 1.5 hours, with seats at around ₹80–120. A reserved car costs more but lets you stop at Simana and the tea gardens. Jeeps run most often in the morning, so do not leave it too late in the day.

faqs.q: Can Indians cross into Nepal near Sukhia Pokhari?
faqs.a: Yes, usually. Indian citizens can cross at Pashupatinagar, near the Simana viewpoint on the Mirik road, to visit Pashupati market without a visa, carrying a passport or voter ID. Children may need a school ID or birth certificate. Foreign nationals generally cannot cross here. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Sukhia Pokhari on the way to Sandakphu?
faqs.a: Yes. The road from Darjeeling to Maneybhanjan, the start of the Singalila Ridge trek to Sandakphu, passes through Sukhia Pokhari, and Maneybhanjan is a short drive on. Trekkers often stop here for supplies and a meal; guides, park entry and Land Rovers are arranged in Maneybhanjan.

faqs.q: Where can we stay near Sukhia Pokhari?
faqs.a: Few rooms in town are of tourist standard, so most people stay nearby: Jorepokhri Tourist Lodge, run by the GTA, 4 km away by the twin ponds; the WBFDC resort and village homestays at Lepchajagat, a few kilometres back toward Ghoom, at about ₹1,500–2,500 per person with meals; or lodges in Maneybhanjan for trekkers.

faqs.q: What is the weather like in Sukhia Pokhari?
faqs.a: Much like Darjeeling, at about 2,100 m. Winter days are cool and nights near freezing from December to February. Spring, March to May, is mild with some haze. The monsoon, June to September, brings heavy rain and mist. October and November are clear and crisp, the best time to visit.

faqs.q: What is there to eat in Sukhia Pokhari?
faqs.a: Simple, cheap hill food: momos, thukpa, chowmein, aloo dum, rice meals and milky tea in roadside kitchens, with a plate of momos at ₹80–150 and a meal at ₹120–200. Sel roti appears around festivals. For bakeries and cafés wait for Darjeeling or Mirik; Sukhia is about honest local food.
